warmup.q: An Iceberg table holds 300,000 payments in 3 files of about 1 MB, one file per day. One MERGE INTO command refunds 30 payments, 10 in each file. With the table's default settings, roughly how much data does that change write?
options: A few KB: only the 30 changed rows
About 3 MB: all three files, written again with the changes
Nothing new: Iceberg edits the 30 rows inside the files
About 1 MB: the one file it rewrites first
warmup.why: The table's data files are Parquet files, which can't be edited in place, and Iceberg's default for changes to rows is copy-on-write: every file that holds a changed row is written again, whole. Here that's all three files, about 3 MB, to change 30 rows. "A few KB" is the tempting answer, because that's what a database would write. It's also what merge-on-read writes instead, and this lesson shows the price readers pay for it.

sections.h: Correcting rows in files that never change: rewrite the file or note the delete
sections.html:
Every evening, a file of refunds reaches the payments company: 30 captured payments whose customers have been paid back. Their status must change from CAPTURED to REFUNDED. In an ordinary database you'd write a query, a command in SQL, the language most databases understand: UPDATE payments SET status = 'REFUNDED' WHERE payment_id IN (...). The database would change 30 rows in place. A warehouse does the same, and Warehouses and dimensional models relied on it to close old versions of a shop.

Our Iceberg table can't. Its rows sit inside Parquet files, a common file format for tables stored by column, and a Parquet file can't be edited. Its column chunks are squeezed. Its footer, a summary at the end of the file, records their sizes, positions and smallest and largest values (Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown, lesson 5). Change one value, and all of that is wrong. So every change is written as new files. Then, as with any Iceberg change, a commit makes them visible: it writes a new snapshot, a version of the table that lists its files, and moves the table's pointer to it.

The command for it is MERGE INTO. It matches a batch of changes to the table on a key, here payment_id, and says what to do with rows that match and rows that don't; the worked example builds one. Under the command, there are two ways to write the files, and the stepper shows both.

Version 1 is copy-on-write. Find every data file that holds a row to change, read it whole, and write a new copy with the change made. The commit swaps the old files for the new ones. In the Try it, 30 refunds spread over three daily files of 100,000 rows rewrote all three: 3.1 MB written and 299,970 unchanged rows copied, to change 30. Readers notice nothing, because the table is still plain data files. That's Iceberg's default, and it suits a table that's read far more often than it changes. It breaks when changes are small and frequent. A feed of corrections every 5 minutes, against files of 512 MB (the size Iceberg aims for by default), rewrites gigabytes an hour to change a few hundred rows.

Version 2 is merge-on-read. Leave the data files alone. Write the new versions of the 30 rows into a small new data file, plus a delete file that says which old rows no longer count. Spark writes position deletes: a data file's path and a row's position in it, such as "row 1,000 of the day 1 file". (Spark, which runs these commands here, is a program that spreads one big job over many computers.) The same 30 refunds wrote 6.4 KB of new rows and 7.4 KB of delete files.

The cost moves to the reader. Every read of a data file must also read the delete files that apply to it, and skip the rows they list. In the notebook, copy-on-write copies the page out again, and merge-on-read pins a slip of corrections to it. The picture breaks at the reader: you'd read a slip once and remember it, while the table's readers apply every delete file again on every read.

Iceberg also has equality deletes, which name a value instead of a position ("payment 1042 is gone"). They're quicker to write and slower to read, because readers compare every row with them.

Format version 3 makes reading cheaper. Over many batches, one data file can collect many position delete files. Version 3 replaces them with deletion vectors. Each data file gets one bitmap, a row of bits with a 1 for each deleted row, stored in a Puffin file (Iceberg's container for extra data like this). A later delete in the same file merges into the same bitmap, so a reader loads at most one small bitmap per data file. In the Try it, the v3 table stored 3 vectors in one 1.7 KB Puffin file.

You choose per table, and per kind of change, with three settings: write.merge.mode, write.update.mode and write.delete.mode, each copy-on-write or merge-on-read. Rare, large changes: copy-on-write. Frequent, small ones: merge-on-read. Merge-on-read sends its reader a bill, though, and next we'll watch it grow.

sections.h: Small files and delete files pile up, until compaction packs them
sections.html:
Merge-on-read and streaming, writing new data in small batches every few minutes as it arrives, have the same side effect: many small files. Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore measured the cost on a plain folder, using Hive, the first popular program for asking SQL questions of files. The same rows as 350 small files took about ten times longer to query than as 7 files. Every file costs an open, a footer read and, on S3 (Amazon's cloud file store), a request with its own wait. A table format removes the folder listing, but not the cost per file. Each data file still has to be opened, and each delete file read and applied.

Watch it build up in the Try it. A stream commits every few minutes, so twelve commits leave twelve small files for one day. Three batches of refunds add three more small data files and twelve delete files. The day's 60,000 rows now live in 15 data files of about 44 KB each. A full read plans 15 file tasks, one per data file, and they must apply 12 delete files. The table also has 15 snapshots, and each one is a little more metadata to read through.

The fix is compaction: rewrite many small files into a few large ones, applying the deletes on the way. In Iceberg, it's a procedure, a built-in command you call from Spark:

CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table => 'pay.stream',
  options => map('min-input-files', '2', 'delete-file-threshold', '1'))

The default strategy, bin-pack, takes one partition at a time (here, one day's files). It packs the rows into files near the target size, 512 MB by default, the way you'd pack odd-sized parcels into as few boxes as possible. min-input-files sets how many small files make a group worth rewriting (5 by default). delete-file-threshold makes any data file with at least that many delete files a candidate. A sort strategy also sorts the rows on the way, which narrows each file's smallest and largest values, so more files can be skipped.

In the Try it, compaction turned 15 data files and 12 delete files into 1 file of about 630 KB. The rows didn't change, and the new snapshot says so. Its operation is replace, which tells readers that the data is the same and only the layout moved.

Compaction is an ordinary commit, so it can race with writers, as in Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg. If a correction lands on a file while compaction is rewriting it, one of the two commits fails its check and has to run again. So run compaction as a scheduled job, partition by partition, and skip the partitions a stream is still writing. On big tables, set partial-progress.enabled, so that one failure doesn't throw away hours of work. Two smaller procedures complete the set: rewrite_position_delete_files packs delete files, and rewrite_manifests repacks the manifests, the metadata files that list the data files, after many small commits.

The table is fast again. Its folder hasn't shrunk at all, though, and next we'll see why.

sections.h: Old versions and orphan files fill the disk until you clean up
sections.html:
Compaction makes the table fast, but not smaller. After the compaction in the Try it, the current snapshot (the table's current version) lists 3 data files, and the data/ folder holds 18. The other 15 are still listed by older snapshots. Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg promised that every snapshot can be read with VERSION AS OF, by time travel, so Iceberg can't delete a file while any snapshot still lists it. Every append, every correction and every compaction leaves the previous files behind.

The clean-up is expiring snapshots. expire_snapshots removes old snapshots from the table's metadata, then deletes every file that only those snapshots used: data files, delete files, and the metadata files that listed them (manifests and manifest lists). By default it expires snapshots older than 5 days, and it always keeps the newest one. In the Try it, expiring everything but the newest snapshot deleted 15 data files, 5 manifests and 5 manifest lists, and data/ went from 18 files to 3.

The price is history. Time travel to an expired snapshot now fails with Cannot find snapshot with ID .... So how long you keep snapshots is a business decision. If someone may ask next month exactly which payments a report read, keep a month of snapshots, or tag that snapshot (give it a name) so that expiry skips it.

One more kind of rubbish has no snapshot at all. A job that crashes after writing its data files, but before its commit, leaves orphan files: files in the table's folder that no snapshot ever listed. Expiry can't find them, because it only deletes files that snapshots name. remove_orphan_files works the other way round. It lists the folder and deletes every file that no snapshot refers to.

That's dangerous in one case. A job that's writing right now has files on disk that aren't committed yet, and they look exactly like orphans. So the procedure only deletes files older than a cut-off, 3 days by default, and refuses any cut-off under 24 hours. In the Try it, a file from a job that crashed three days ago was removed, and a file being written right now was kept.

Run all three on a schedule: compact, then expire, then remove orphans now and then. On object storage, deletes cost requests too, and the storage bill only drops once expiry has run. Skipping all this is easy, because nothing fails. Every query stays right while the table gets slower and its folder grows, until a daily report that took two minutes takes many times longer.

So far, every commit has trusted one pointer to swap safely. Next, we'll look at who holds it.

aside.title: If I delete a customer's payments, are they really gone?
aside.html: Not from the disk, at first. A DELETE commits a new snapshot that no longer shows the rows, but older snapshots still list the files that hold them, and time travel can read them back. On a merge-on-read table, even the current data file still holds the rows, hidden by a delete file. The bytes are gone only once compaction has rewritten those files without the rows, and expiry has deleted the old files. Laws that give people the right to have their data erased mean you need both jobs, on a schedule you can state.

sections.h: The catalog: who holds the pointer, and how it swaps
sections.html:
Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg ended every commit with a compare-and-swap of one pointer: "the table is now v4.metadata.json, if it's still v3". A compare-and-swap changes a value only if it still holds the value you read. Whatever stores that pointer, and makes the swap safe, is the catalog. It also answers the first question every engine (a program that runs questions over data) asks: which tables exist, and where is each one's current metadata?

Version 1 is the Hadoop catalog that lesson used, named after Hadoop, an older big data system. The pointer is the newest metadata file in a folder, and the swap is a rename that fails if the target already exists. That needs a file system whose rename is all-or-nothing. Your laptop has one, and so does HDFS, Hadoop's file system. Object storage doesn't, so this catalog is for learning.

Version 2 puts the pointer in a database. Hive keeps its tables in the Hive Metastore, a service in front of a database. It can hold Iceberg's pointer too, as a property of the table. Iceberg's JDBC catalog is the simplest to read. (JDBC is Java's standard way to talk to a database.) It keeps one row per table in a table called iceberg_tables, and a commit is a single SQL statement:

UPDATE iceberg_tables
SET metadata_location = ?, previous_metadata_location = ?
WHERE catalog_name = ? AND table_namespace = ? AND table_name = ?
  AND metadata_location = ?        -- the version this writer started from

Each ? is filled in with the writer's values. If another writer moved the pointer first, the last condition matches no row, zero rows change, and Iceberg throws CommitFailedException. It's the check a careful program makes on any shared row: change it only if nobody changed it since you read it. The Try it runs this catalog on SQLite, a small database kept in one file, and shows the row after each commit.

Version 2 has a cost. Every engine needs the database's driver (the library that talks to it), its password and the right Iceberg library version. Version 3 puts the catalog behind a web API, a set of addresses that programs send requests to. That's the Iceberg REST catalog protocol, so that engines talk to it with ordinary HTTP requests, the kind a browser sends. The client asks GET /v1/namespaces/pay/tables/payments and gets back the table's metadata, pointer included. To commit, it sends a POST to the same address with a list of requirements, such as "the current snapshot is still 5087...", and a list of updates. The server checks the requirements and applies the updates all at once, or answers 409 Conflict, the web's code for "someone changed it first". Because the server stands between the engines and the storage, it can hand each client short-lived storage passwords for that one table, and apply access rules in one place. Spark and DuckDB, a small analytics database that runs inside your own program, both speak this protocol, and so do most other engines.

You don't write a REST catalog yourself. Apache Polaris, a free catalog server and an Apache top-level project since 2026, implements it. Unity Catalog, a free catalog first built by Databricks (a company that sells a data platform built on Spark), has served it since release 0.7. Cloud providers run their own. Pick one that every engine you use can reach.

Iceberg isn't the only format that commits this way. Next, we'll set it beside its two rivals, and a newcomer that asks why the metadata isn't kept in a database already.

try.title: Read the catalog's row
steps: From the labs folder, run CatalogDemo. It sets up a second Spark catalog, shop, of type jdbc, backed by the SQLite file bigdata/build/l10/catalog.db. It creates a table, appends twice and prints the catalog's row after each step. Then two writers load the same version, and both try to commit.
Predict what writer B's commit does, and what the row says afterwards.
Open the catalog yourself, from the labs folder: sqlite3 -line bigdata/build/l10/catalog.db "SELECT * FROM iceberg_tables". (macOS comes with sqlite3; on Linux, install the sqlite3 package.)

code.title: CatalogDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l12.demo import org.apache.iceberg.HasTableOperations import org.apache.iceberg.TableMetadata import org.apache.iceberg.catalog.TableIdentifier import org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.CommitFailedException import org.apache.iceberg.spark.Spark3Util import java.io.File import java.sql.DriverManager /** * An Iceberg JDBC catalog whose database is one SQLite file. Prints the catalog's row for the * table after each commit, then shows a commit from a stale version being refused. */ fun main() { val db = File("build/l10/catalog.db").apply { delete() } val spark = demoSpark( "spark.sql.catalog.shop" to "org.apache.iceberg.spark.SparkCatalog", "spark.sql.catalog.shop.type" to "jdbc", "spark.sql.catalog.shop.uri" to "jdbc:sqlite:${db.absolutePath}", "spark.sql.catalog.shop.warehouse" to File(WAREHOUSE, "shop").absolutePath, ) fun catalogRow(label: String) = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:sqlite:${db.absolutePath}").use { c -> c.createStatement().executeQuery( "SELECT table_namespace, table_name, metadata_location, previous_metadata_location FROM iceberg_tables" ).use { rs -> while (rs.next()) { fun name(i: Int) = rs.getString(i)?.substringAfterLast('/')?.replace(Regex("^(\\d+)-[0-9a-f-]{36}"), "$1-<uuid>") ?: "null" println("$label: ${rs.getString(1)}.${rs.getString(2)} -> ${name(3)} (previous: ${name(4)})") } } } spark.sql("CREATE TABLE shop.pay.payments ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))") catalogRow("after CREATE TABLE") payments(spark, 0, 1_000).writeTo("shop.pay.payments").append() catalogRow("after the 1st append") payments(spark, 1_000, 1_000).writeTo("shop.pay.payments").append() catalogRow("after the 2nd append") // two writers load the same version; A commits first, then B tries from its stale base val catalog = Spark3Util.loadIcebergCatalog(spark, "shop") val id = TableIdentifier.of("pay", "payments") val a = (catalog.loadTable(id) as HasTableOperations).operations() val b = (catalog.loadTable(id) as HasTableOperations).operations() val baseA = a.current() val baseB = b.current() a.commit(baseA, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseA).setProperties(mapOf("owner" to "settlement")).build()) catalogRow("after writer A's commit") try { b.commit(baseB, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseB).setProperties(mapOf("owner" to "fraud")).build()) } catch (e: CommitFailedException) { println("writer B, from the old version: CommitFailedException: ${e.message!!.replace(Regex("/\\S+/"), "")}") } catalogRow("after writer B's attempt") println("rows: %,d".format(spark.table("shop.pay.payments").count())) spark.stop() }

try.expect:
after CREATE TABLE: pay.payments -> 00000-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: null)
after the 1st append: pay.payments -> 00001-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00000-<uuid>.metadata.json)
after the 2nd append: pay.payments -> 00002-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00001-<uuid>.metadata.json)
after writer A's commit: pay.payments -> 00003-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00002-<uuid>.metadata.json)
writer B, from the old version: CommitFailedException: Cannot commit: stale table metadata
after writer B's attempt: pay.payments -> 00003-<uuid>.metadata.json (previous: 00002-<uuid>.metadata.json)
rows: 2,000

Each commit wrote a new metadata file and moved the row's metadata_location to it, keeping the old one in previous_metadata_location. Writer A's commit moved the pointer from 00002 to 00003. Writer B started from 00002 too. Its UPDATE ... WHERE metadata_location = <00002> matched no row, so Iceberg threw CommitFailedException, and the row didn't move. The table still has 2,000 rows. Your sqlite3 output shows the same row with full paths, something like this (paths shortened):

              catalog_name: shop
           table_namespace: pay
                table_name: payments
         metadata_location: .../warehouse/shop/pay/payments/metadata/00003-8190629d-....metadata.json
previous_metadata_location: .../warehouse/shop/pay/payments/metadata/00002-3bfa617f-....metadata.json

That row is the whole catalog for this table. Delete it and every engine loses the table, even though every file is still on disk.

sections.h: Delta Lake, Hudi and DuckLake: the same trade, made differently
sections.html:
Iceberg isn't the only table format. Delta Lake and Apache Hudi make the same trade with different files, and DuckLake moves the metadata into a database. All of them keep Parquet data files that are never edited, list them in metadata, and commit with one step that either happens or doesn't.

Delta Lake, the format Databricks created, keeps a log instead of a tree. Every commit is a numbered JSON file (JSON is a text format of names and values) in a folder called _delta_log/. A file such as 00000000000000000007.json lists the data files that commit added and removed. A reader replays the log: it reads it in order, starting from the newest checkpoint, a Parquet summary of the whole state that Delta writes every few commits. A commit means "create file number 8, if it doesn't exist yet". Two writers can't both create it, so one wins.

On S3, that's exactly what If-None-Match has offered since 2024 (Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg). Yet Delta's S3 documentation still asks for a single writing program per table, or a lock table in DynamoDB, Amazon's database service. Delta has copy-on-write, merge-on-read through deletion vectors, MERGE INTO and compaction (OPTIMIZE): the same ideas under other names. It's the default format on Databricks, and 4.4.1, from October 2026, is the current release. Its UniForm feature writes Iceberg metadata next to Delta's, so Iceberg readers can read a Delta table.

Apache Hudi, another free table format, grew up applying a stream of changes copied from other databases, a feed called change data capture (CDC). It names the two ways of writing as table types, COPY_ON_WRITE and MERGE_ON_READ. It also keeps an index from each row's key to its file, so a change finds its row without reading everything. Hudi 1.2.1 is current. Choose it when your work is mostly changes by key from such a feed, and your team already knows it.

DuckLake, from the makers of DuckDB, asks a sharper question. If a catalog is a database anyway, why keep the rest of the metadata in files? DuckLake 1.0 came out in April 2026, and 1.1 ships with DuckDB 2.0. It stores snapshots, columns, file lists and statistics as rows in a SQL database, and keeps the data in Parquet. The database can be PostgreSQL (a free database program many companies run), SQLite or DuckDB. A commit is one database transaction, a group of changes that happen all together or not at all. So a small change writes a few rows, instead of a manifest, a manifest list and a metadata file, and one commit can cover several tables.

The trade: every reader needs that database, commits can't come faster than it allows (PostgreSQL manages thousands a second), and far fewer engines read DuckLake than Iceberg.

For a payments company starting today, Iceberg with a REST catalog is the safe default, because the most engines read and write it. Choosing an engine: DuckDB, Spark, Trino and friends, the last lesson of this track, relies on it. Pick Delta if you run on Databricks, and keep DuckLake in mind for a small team that lives in DuckDB.

opening:
Picture a shop that keeps its sales in notebooks, in pen, one page per day. One evening, 30 refunds come in, 10 from each of the last three days. You can't rub out ink. So you either copy the three pages out again with the changes, or leave them alone and pin a slip of corrections to each.

A table in Apache Iceberg, a free format for tables made of plain files, faces this choice whenever a row changes, because its files are never edited. The command looks like a database's UPDATE, which changes rows in place, so it's easy to expect a database's cost. The real bill can be hundreds of times bigger, or arrive later, at every read.

In Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg, we built such a table, where every change adds files and moves one pointer. In this lesson, we'll correct rows both ways, clean up the small files and old versions that pile up, and see who holds that pointer. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with sales books written in pen, and 30 refunds that couldn't be rubbed out. An Iceberg table makes the same choice: copy the pages out again, or pin on a slip of corrections and tidy up later. Either way, someone has to clear away the old pages.

Run CompactionDemo, then open labs/bigdata/build/l10/warehouse/pay/stream/data and count the files in its day folder. The current snapshot lists one of them. Every other file there is waiting for expiry.

Next, we'll schedule jobs like these, run them in the right order, and find out what has to be true before a job can safely run twice.

  metadata/

    snap-5087...-3f2c....avro     new manifest list: old manifests + new one

b.label: Delta Lake
b.title: a numbered log of JSON commits
b.html:
payments/
  dt=2026-11-03/
    part-00000-....parquet        new data file
  _delta_log/
    00000000000000000006.json     earlier commits
    00000000000000000007.json     new: {"add": {"path": "dt=.../part-....parquet", ...}}

    000...010.checkpoint.parquet  every few commits: the whole state, for fast replay

        only if no one created it first

compare.note: Both formats write the data file first, where no reader can see it, and both commit with one step that fails if someone else got there first. Iceberg's step is a swap in a catalog, and a reader starts from the catalog's pointer and walks down a tree. Delta's step is creating the next numbered file, and a reader lists _delta_log/, loads the newest checkpoint and replays the JSON files after it. Iceberg's manifests can be shared between snapshots and skipped by their partition ranges before they're opened; Delta's log is easier to read by hand. Delta 4 can also let a catalog coordinate commits, and its UniForm feature writes Iceberg metadata beside the log.

worked.title: Apply the evening refund file with one MERGE

steps.say: Stage the corrections as a view, a saved query you can use like a table, with one row per payment. The bank's file can list the same payment twice, say a refund and then a correction that cancels it. MERGE allows at most one change row per table row, so keep only the newest row for each payment_id.
steps.code: CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW corrections AS SELECT payment_id, status, amount_cents, created_at, merchant_id, card_country, currency FROM ( SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_id ORDER BY received_at DESC) AS rn FROM refund_file ) WHERE rn = 1;

steps.say: Write the MERGE. Match on the key, delete voided payments (a void cancels a payment as if it never happened), update everything else that matched, and insert payments the table has never seen, such as captures that arrived late. Spark runs this as a join of the small view against the table. Copying the corrections to every machine (a broadcast) and skipping files by created_at keep it cheap.
steps.code: MERGE INTO lake.pay.payments t USING corrections c ON t.payment_id = c.payment_id WHEN MATCHED AND c.status = 'VOID' THEN DELETE WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.status = c.status, t.amount_cents = c.amount_cents WHEN NOT MATCHED AND c.status <> 'VOID' THEN INSERT *;

steps.say: If you skipped the first step and a payment appears twice, Spark stops before writing anything, with MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION: one table row matched several change rows, and Spark won't guess which one wins. Nothing is committed, so you can fix the view and run it again.
steps.code:
-- [MERGE_CARDINALITY_VIOLATION] The ON search condition of the MERGE statement
-- matched a single row from the target table with multiple rows of the source table.

steps.say: Check what the commit did. The snapshot's summary records it: for a merge-on-read table, the delete files added and the rows inserted; for copy-on-write, the files removed and the rows copied.
steps.code: SELECT summary['spark.merge-into.num-target-rows-updated'] AS updated, summary['spark.merge-into.num-target-rows-deleted'] AS voided, summary['spark.merge-into.num-target-rows-inserted'] AS inserted, summary['added-delete-files'] AS delete_files FROM lake.pay.payments.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 1;

steps.say: Leave the table healthy for tomorrow. The maintenance job compacts the partitions the merge touched, then expires snapshots older than the time you keep them.
steps.code: CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files( table => 'pay.payments', where => 'created_at >= "2026-11-01"', options => map('delete-file-threshold', '1')); CALL lake.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'pay.payments', older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-10-08 00:00:00');

lab.title: Correct payments, then compact and clean up
steps: From the labs folder, run the tests with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code, and all seven fail for now on TODOs. Each test class makes a Hadoop catalog called l12 in a temporary folder, and the tests read the snapshot summaries, the data_files and delete_files metadata tables, and the files on disk.
Write PaymentCorrections.create: the payments table, grouped by days(created_at), with four table settings: the format version and the three write.*.mode settings.

Write applyCorrections: register the corrections as a temporary view, run one MERGE INTO with the three clauses its KDoc (the comment above the function) lists, and return the newest snapshot's summary. The tests check that copy-on-write removed 3 data files and copied 2,997 rows, that merge-on-read on v2 wrote 3 position delete files and touched no data file, and that v3 wrote 3 deletion vectors in one Puffin file.

Write TableMaintenance.health from the metadata tables, then compact and expireSnapshots with the procedures. The test table has 12 small data files and 3 delete files. After compact, it must have one file per day and no delete files, with the same rows.
The expiry test counts Parquet files on disk before and after, and checks that time travel to the first snapshot fails once that snapshot has expired.
hints: spark.sql("SELECT summary FROM $name.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at DESC LIMIT 1").first().getJavaMap<String, String>(0).toMap().

The catalog is name.substringBefore('.'), and the procedure's table is name.substringAfter('.'): CALL l12.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'ops.t', options => map('min-input-files', '2', 'delete-file-threshold', '1', 'remove-dangling-deletes', 'true')). Read the result with first().getAs<Int>("rewritten_data_files_count").

expire_snapshots takes older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-11-07 10:15:00.000' (in the session's time zone, spark.sql.session.timeZone) and retain_last => 1. Its result has deleted_data_files_count as a Long.

drill.title: Corrections and maintenance from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write: the table settings that make an Iceberg table use merge-on-read for MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE on format v3; a MERGE INTO that applies refunds from a view refunds(payment_id, amount_cents); and the three maintenance calls, in the order you'd schedule them. Then say which of the three can make time travel fail.

answer.html: ALTER TABLE lake.pay.payments SET TBLPROPERTIES ( 'format-version' = '3', 'write.merge.mode' = 'merge-on-read', 'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read', 'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read'); MERGE INTO lake.pay.payments t USING refunds r ON t.payment_id = r.payment_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.status = 'REFUNDED', t.amount_cents = r.amount_cents; -- 1. compact: fewer, bigger files, deletes applied (a 'replace' snapshot) CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'pay.payments', options => map('delete-file-threshold', '1')); -- 2. expire: drop old snapshots and the files only they used (ends time travel to them) CALL lake.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'pay.payments', older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-10-08 00:00:00'); -- 3. orphans: files no snapshot ever listed, older than the cut-off (3 days by default) CALL lake.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'pay.payments'); -- only expire_snapshots ends time travel: compaction keeps the old snapshots, -- and orphan files were never in any snapshot

recap: Data files are never edited, so a change to a row writes new files. Copy-on-write rewrites every file that holds a changed row: slow writes, simple reads, and Iceberg's default.
Merge-on-read writes the new rows plus delete files: position deletes (file, row) in format v2, one deletion vector per data file in v3. Writes are cheap, and readers merge until compaction.

rewrite_data_files packs small files and applies deletes in a replace snapshot. expire_snapshots deletes files that only old snapshots used, and ends time travel to them. remove_orphan_files deletes uncommitted leftovers older than a safe cut-off.

The catalog holds each table's pointer and does the compare-and-swap: a rename (Hadoop), a conditional UPDATE (JDBC), or an HTTP commit with requirements (the REST protocol, served by Polaris, Unity Catalog and the cloud providers' catalogs).
Delta Lake commits numbered JSON log files, Hudi aims at changes by key from a feed, and DuckLake keeps all of its metadata in a SQL database. Iceberg with a REST catalog is the safe default.
The limit: none of this runs by itself. Compaction, expiry and the orphan clean-up are jobs that someone has to schedule, in the right order, and make safe to run twice.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why your merge-on-read payments table needs three scheduled jobs, by following one batch of 30 refunds from the MERGE to the day its old files disappear.
explain.answer: The MERGE can't edit Parquet files. On a merge-on-read table, it writes the refunded versions of the 30 rows into a small new data file, plus a delete file for each data file it touched, saying which old rows no longer count. On format v3 that's one deletion vector per data file. The commit is cheap, but every reader of those days now opens the data files, the new small files and the delete files, and merges them. After a day of batches, that's dozens of extra files per partition. The first job, compaction (rewrite_data_files), reads each partition's files with their deletes and writes a few clean, large files in a replace snapshot, so reads are fast again. But nothing has been deleted yet: the snapshots from before compaction still list the old files, which is what makes time travel work. The second job, expire_snapshots, removes snapshots older than the time we keep them, and deletes every file only they used. From then on, time travel to those snapshots fails, so that time has to cover what anyone may ask about later. The third job, remove_orphan_files, catches files that no snapshot ever listed, like the output of a MERGE that crashed before its commit. It only touches files older than a cut-off, 3 days by default, because files of a job that's still running look exactly like orphans.

deeper.html:
Equality deletes in detail. A writer that only knows a key, such as a Flink job applying changes from a feed, can write "delete every row where payment_id = 1042" without finding the row first. (Flink is a program for processing streams of events as they arrive.) Every reader of every older data file in that partition must then check its rows against those values. Iceberg applies an equality delete only to data files with a lower sequence number, meaning files written before it. Compact tables that receive them often.

Isolation for changes to rows. Appends could always be applied again after losing a race. A MERGE read some files and decided what to change from them, so if another commit changed those same files first, applying it again could lose an update. Iceberg's write.merge.isolation-level (and its update and delete cousins) defaults to serializable. Before committing, the writer checks whether any conflicting files were added or deleted since it started, and fails if so. snapshot isolation checks less and lets more work run at the same time.

The REST protocol keeps growing. Besides loading and committing tables, servers can plan reads on the server side (Iceberg 1.11), and Iceberg 1.12 added idempotency keys, so a client whose commit request timed out can retry without committing twice. Hive's documentation describes a REST catalog served by the Hive Metastore itself, so an existing metastore can speak the new protocol.

Version notes. Delta 4.4 supports Spark 4.0.1, 4.1 and 4.2, but its UniForm module doesn't support Spark 4.2 yet. Delta 4.3 added Unity Catalog's Delta REST API, part of a move to catalog-managed tables, where the catalog rather than the log in storage coordinates commits. Hudi 1.2 added VECTOR, VARIANT and BLOB types and support for Lance, a newer column file format aimed at machine-learning data, and ships bundles for Spark 3.3 to 4.1.

DuckLake's trick for small changes. With data inlining, inserts below a row limit are stored as rows in the catalog database instead of as tiny Parquet files, and a flush writes them to Parquet later. That attacks the small-files problem where it starts.
